finding.claim: The caller's identity is taken straight from the client-supplied header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing in the code authenticates it, strips it or signs it. Any client can send the header with another user's name and inherit that user's grants. This can delete or rename that user's files. It is exploitable whenever the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that overwrites or strips this header. No such proxy exists in this repo.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, set by any unauthenticated remote client
finding.sink: ensure_allowed/is_allowed in acl.py:5 compares g.user against resource grants. The result gates `del STORE[fid]` (views.py:18) and the rename write (views.py:27).

trace.note: before_request sets g.user from the raw header with no verification
is_allowed looks up grants[user] using the spoofed name
POST /files/<fid>/rename uses the same spoofed identity and then writes f['name'] at line 27

finding.guards_checked: The ACL check is enforced correctly: ensure_allowed aborts with 403, and rename returns on failure. A missing header gives g.user=None, which has no grants, so it is denied. No signature, session or token verification exists. No proxy or middleware in the repo strips or overwrites the header. Not verified: whether a deployment-level proxy does this. Also seen and not reported: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown id (a 500, not a vulnerability).

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 and is_allowed (views.py:25) is tested, but both only check the spoofable g.user. No header stripping, signing or authentication exists in the repo, which has only acl.py and views.py.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 sets g.user from the raw X-Session-User-Verified header, so any client can send a victim's name and pass the ACL checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 (acl.py:5) to reach `del STORE[fid]` (views.py:18) or the rename write (views.py:27); the only caveat is that a deployment proxy outside this repo might strip the header.
